free_tier.stated: Free tier shown on puter.com as '25 MB Storage' (the 100 GB / 500 GB / 2 TB figures on that page are the paid tiers — verified by reading the raw HTML, not the rendered summary). Developer-side cost is $0: 'Puter doesn't charge developers for infrastructure. Storage, database, and AI usage are metered to each signed-in user's own Puter account.'

retention.stated: no retention statement was extracted from the seed's quota and limits prose; absence here is a gap in this conversion, not a vendor claim that retention is unlimited
retention.notes: extraction found no retention clause; the seed's limits text may still state one, see extras.limits_verbatim

egress.terms: Not metered per-GB to the developer; metered to the end user's Puter allowance. No egress line found.

tooling: Puter.js — a single <script> tag or the @heyputer/puter.js npm module, keyless. puter.fs.write / read / mkdir give a browser-side filesystem API; auth is 'sign in with Puter'. No S3/WebDAV/SFTP shim.
chaining: The interesting multiplier is the opposite of the usual one: because storage is metered to each *signed-in user's* account, an app with N users gets N x (that user's allowance) and the developer pays nothing. But the free allowance per user is 25 MB, so the chain only works if the app also controls the user accounts — i.e. it is a way to make storage free for an app's users, not a way to get 10 TiB.

limits_note: per-object-cap: not documented, but the free allowance is 25 MB total, which is the real cap. Request-rate: the vendor states that 'Anti-abuse, rate limiting, and fraud detection are also built into the Puter account layer, so bots and fake sign-ups are filtered before they reach your app'. In neutral terms, its signup layer screens for excess use and automated signups, so free identities are NOT unlimited here. Retention: not documented.

reliability_note: Explicitly blocks the several-accounts route: Puter markets that 'usage is metered to each user's own account, so a bad actor has no free resources to farm', plus automated-signup filtering. That removes the second-account allowance this niche usually relies on.
